title: Savoring joy
hook: Thoreau sits in his sunny doorway from sunrise till noon and grows 'like corn in the night'
tomorrow: how did one monk know his friend's news before he heard it?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: joy is allowed. This week's lines come back in the games: call out, the first seven days, feathers, beautifully, it rises. Today, how to stay with a good moment.
screen: `JOY IS ALLOWED.` → `THIS WEEK'S LINES.` → `STAYING WITH IT.`

segments.voice: A sunset gets photographed, and looked at later on a screen. Henry David Thoreau, living in his cabin by Walden Pond, did something else. In Walden, he writes that on some summer mornings, after his bath, he sat in his sunny doorway from sunrise till noon, among the pines and hickories, in undisturbed solitude and stillness, while the birds sang around him or flitted through the house. Hours. Doing, by most measures, nothing.
screen: `A SUNSET, ON A SCREEN.` → `THOREAU'S SUNNY DOORWAY.` → `SUNRISE TILL NOON.`

segments.voice: Then comes the line that makes it a teaching: "I grew in those seasons like corn in the night." He insists those hours weren't time taken out of his life; they were far better, he says, than any work of the hands would have been. And from the same chapter: "I love a broad margin to my life." That's a Walden idea worth keeping: a good life needs margin, unfilled space around the work, the way a page needs white space around the words. Savoring happens in the margin. You don't add more to a good moment. You give it room. And look at his picture: Thoreau compared himself to corn, which does its growing in the dark, when nobody's watching. So savoring isn't a technique. It's a margin, kept on purpose. That's this week, too. It began in suffering: calling out, sitting in silence with someone, a hope with feathers, Jacob's beautiful patience, a wall rising stretch by stretch. And it turned toward joy that's allowed. Savoring is how that joy gets to stay a little longer.
screen: `LIKE CORN IN THE NIGHT.` · `A BROAD MARGIN TO MY LIFE.` · `GIVE THE MOMENT ROOM.` · `FROM SUFFERING TO JOY.` · then, large: `SAVOR.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and bring back one good moment from this week; small is fine. Stay in it the way Thoreau stayed in his doorway: the light, the sound, who was there. Don't explain it to yourself; let it take up the whole margin.
Savoring joy: giving a good moment room to stay, the broad margin Thoreau loved.
Hold onto this: savor, and leave a broad margin around the good. That's the week, done.
